overview.summary: Radiologists are doctors who use medical imaging, such as X-rays, ultrasound, CT and MRI scans, to help diagnose illness and injury, and some carry out image-guided procedures.
overview.problems: They find out what is happening inside the body without surgery, helping other doctors choose the right treatment.
overview.worksWith: Other doctors and surgeons, radiographers who take the images, nurses, physicists and patients.
overview.workplaces: Hospitals and imaging centres, mostly in reading rooms with screens, and in procedure rooms for some interventional work.

timeline.title: Review urgent requests
timeline.description: The radiologist checks which scans need to be read first.

timeline.title: Reading images
timeline.description: The radiologist studies scans carefully on screen, compares them with earlier images and notes the findings.
timeline.why: Careful viewing finds small but important changes.

timeline.title: Writing reports
timeline.description: The radiologist dictates or writes clear reports that tell the referring doctor what was found.
timeline.why: The report guides the patient's treatment.

timeline.title: Discussing cases
timeline.description: The radiologist talks with surgeons and other specialists in team meetings.
timeline.why: Images are more useful when read together with the patient's story.

timeline.title: Procedures or supervision
timeline.description: Some radiologists perform image-guided procedures or supervise scans and radiation safety.
timeline.why: Imaging can guide treatment as well as diagnosis.

timeline.title: On-call work
timeline.description: Emergency scans may need to be read at night.
timeline.why: Urgent cases arrive at any hour.

responsibilities: Interpreting medical images and reporting results
Advising other doctors on which scan is best
Making sure imaging is safe, including radiation protection
Performing image-guided procedures in some roles
challenges: Long periods of concentration are needed when looking at screens.
Missing a finding can have serious consequences.
Scan volumes are high and there is time pressure.
Many roles involve limited direct contact with patients.
Training is long: medical school followed by specialist training.
workEnvironment: Hospital reading rooms with screens, often dimly lit, and imaging departments. Much of the work is seated at a workstation, with meetings and some procedures. Some roles include on-call duties.
tradeoffs: Pressure to be accurate and fast
Pay and conditions that vary by country and setting

activity.title: Practise careful observation with spot-the-difference puzzles
steps: Find a spot-the-difference puzzle with two similar pictures.
Study each picture in a set pattern, such as left to right and top to bottom.
Time yourself and record how many differences you find.
Read a patient information page about how X-rays or scans work, from a trusted site such as RadiologyInfo.org.
Note whether close observation felt interesting.
activity.outcome: You practise systematic looking and explaining how imaging works, which radiologists use every day.
activity.safety: This is for learning only. Never try to read or interpret anyone's medical images or give medical advice, and talk to a doctor about real health concerns.

source: Written by Futurixia from general knowledge of how this profession works. It is illustrative and is not based on interviews or surveys.
